steps: Mineral nutrition is the process by which plants absorb and use mineral nutrients for their growth and development.
items.finalAnswer: Mineral nutrition is the absorption and use of mineral nutrients by plants for growth and development.

steps: Macronutrients are mineral nutrients required by plants in large amounts.
Examples of macronutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.
Micronutrients are mineral nutrients required by plants in very small amounts.
Examples of micronutrients are iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper, molybdenum and chlorine.
items.finalAnswer: Macronutrients are needed in large amounts, while micronutrients are needed in very small amounts; nitrogen and magnesium are examples of macronutrients, and iron and zinc are examples of micronutrients.

steps: Nitrogen is needed for the formation of proteins and other important compounds in plants.
Magnesium is a component of chlorophyll and is therefore essential for photosynthesis.
items.finalAnswer: Nitrogen is needed to form proteins, while magnesium is a component of chlorophyll.

steps: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
The three types of transpiration are stomatal transpiration, cuticular transpiration and lenticular transpiration.
Stomatal transpiration occurs through stomata, cuticular transpiration through the cuticle, and lenticular transpiration through lenticels.
items.finalAnswer: Transpiration is water loss as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant; its types are stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.

steps: Transpirational pull is the suction force produced by transpiration from the leaves.
It helps in the upward movement of water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to the leaves through the xylem.
items.finalAnswer: Transpirational pull helps transport water and dissolved mineral salts upward from the roots to the leaves.

steps: No, transpiration is not wholly harmful; it is an important process in plants.
It produces transpirational pull, which helps in the upward transport of water and dissolved mineral salts from roots to leaves.
It also helps cool the plant.
items.finalAnswer: Transpiration is important because it aids the upward transport of water and mineral salts and cools the plant.

steps: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to the aerial parts of the plant.
Phloem transports prepared food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Xylem tissue is mainly made up of dead cells, whereas phloem tissue is mainly made up of living cells.
items.finalAnswer: Xylem transports water and minerals upward and is mainly made of dead cells; phloem transports food and is mainly made of living cells.

steps: Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant in the form of water vapour; guttation is the loss of water in the form of liquid droplets.
Transpiration occurs mainly through stomata, and also through the cuticle and lenticels; guttation occurs through hydathodes, usually at the edges or tips of leaves.
Transpiration usually occurs during the day, whereas guttation commonly occurs at night or early in the morning.
Transpiration is caused by evaporation of water, whereas guttation is caused by root pressure.
items.finalAnswer: Transpiration is loss of water vapour mainly through stomata, while guttation is loss of liquid water through hydathodes, usually due to root pressure.
